Treasure Island was written by Robert Louis Stevenson and first published in 1883. It is one of the most famous adventure stories ever told, and it shaped how the whole world imagines pirates: treasure maps marked with an X, parrots crying on shoulders, and buried chests of gold. This retelling keeps the heart of the tale for young readers.

My name is Jim Hawkins, and I shall tell you the whole tale of Treasure Island. It began at my father's inn by the sea, where I helped serve the guests. One grey morning, a strange old sailor came tramping up to our door, a sabre scar on his cheek and a heavy sea chest hauled behind him. He took a room, and he stayed.

image.note: A weather-beaten old sailor with a scarred cheek arriving at a lonely seaside inn, dragging a sea chest; young Jim watching from the doorway

pages.text: He was a grim, silent man who sang wild songs of the sea and frightened the other guests. He paid me a fourpenny piece each month to watch the road and warn him if ever a sailor with one leg should appear. Who this one-legged man was, I did not know, but the old captain feared him more than anything on Earth.

image.note: The old captain gripping Jim by the shoulder, pressing a coin into his hand, eyes darting to the road; fearful, secretive

pages.text: Other strange sailors began to come. One day a blind beggar tapped his way to the inn and pressed something into the captain's hand, then hurried off. The captain opened it, went white as chalk, and gasped that they had given him the black spot, a pirate's sentence of doom. Then he clutched his chest, cried out, and fell dead upon the floor.

image.note: The old captain staring in horror at a small black paper mark in his palm, one hand at his chest; a blind beggar hurrying away outside

pages.text: My father had died only days before, and now this. My mother and I knew the captain owed us money, so we opened his sea chest to take only what we were due. And there, beneath his clothes and pistols, wrapped in oilcloth, we found a packet of papers. We had barely seized it when we heard the tap-tap of the blind man returning up the road.

image.note: Jim and his mother kneeling over an open sea chest by candlelight, lifting out an oilcloth packet; tense, hurried

pages.text: We fled just in time as the pirates ransacked the inn behind us. Safe at last, I opened the packet and found a map. It showed an island, with hills and woods and coves marked upon it, and there, in red ink, three crosses, and the words that set my heart racing: bulk of treasure here. It was a chart to a fortune in buried gold.

image.note: Jim unrolling an old map on a table, an island drawn with three red crosses; a squire and a doctor leaning in, amazed

pages.text: I showed the map to two good men, Squire Trelawney and Doctor Livesey. The squire, a bold and hearty gentleman, at once declared we should sail and find the gold. He would buy a ship, hire a crew, and take me along as cabin boy. Doctor Livesey warned him to be careful whom he trusted, but the squire was already dreaming of treasure.

image.note: The cheerful, portly squire slapping the table with delight; the calm, careful doctor raising a warning hand; Jim between them

pages.text: In the port town, the squire hired a fine ship, the Hispaniola, and a crew. Much of the crew was gathered by the ship's cook, a clever one-legged man named Long John Silver, who kept a parrot on his shoulder that cried out, "Pieces of eight!" I liked Silver at once, for he was merry and kind to me. I did not yet remember the captain's warning about a sailor with one leg.

image.note: The cheerful one-legged Long John Silver in a ship galley, a green parrot on his shoulder, welcoming young Jim; warm, disarming

pages.text: We set sail on a bright morning, the Hispaniola cutting through blue water towards the far-off island. For days all seemed well. Silver told me grand tales of the sea, the sails filled, and I thought myself the luckiest boy alive. But a ship is a small world, and secrets do not stay hidden long upon the open water.

image.note: The Hispaniola under full sail on a bright blue sea, Jim at the rail gazing ahead; adventure, open horizon

chapters.title: What I Heard in the Apple Barrel

pages.text: One warm evening, I climbed into the big apple barrel on deck to fetch a fruit, and I curled up at the bottom of it, half asleep. Then Long John Silver sat down close beside the barrel, not knowing I was there, and began to talk low with two other sailors. What I heard turned my blood to ice.

image.note: Jim crouched hidden inside a large apple barrel on deck, eyes wide, listening; Silver seated just outside, unaware

pages.text: Silver was no honest cook. He was a pirate, and the crew he had gathered were mostly pirates too. Their plan was to let us find the treasure, and then to murder every honest man aboard and sail away rich. The one-legged man the old captain had feared was Silver himself. I had trusted the very worst of them.

image.note: Silver's face turned hard and cruel as he plots quietly with two rough sailors; the friendly mask slipped; sinister

pages.text: The moment I could, I slipped out and warned the squire, the doctor and the captain. Now we knew the truth, but we were outnumbered. There were only a few of us honest men against a shipful of pirates. We agreed to keep our knowledge secret, to watch and wait, and to strike only when the time was right.

image.note: Jim whispering urgently to the doctor, squire and ship's captain in a cabin; grave faces; a secret alliance

pages.text: At last the island rose out of the sea, grey and wooded, with strange twisted hills. The pirates grew restless and hard to command. To calm them, Silver let some of the men go ashore. I made a sudden, reckless choice and slipped into a boat with them, and then, as it touched land, I leapt out and ran alone into the woods to escape the pirates.

image.note: A wooded, hilly island seen from the ship; Jim leaping from a beached boat and dashing into thick trees; bold, alone

pages.text: Deep in the woods, a wild figure sprang out at me, ragged and burned brown by the sun. I was terrified, but he fell to his knees and begged for kindness. He was Ben Gunn, a sailor marooned alone on the island three long years before, left behind by pirates. He had lived on goats and berries, and longed only to go home.

image.note: A ragged, wild-haired marooned man, Ben Gunn, kneeling before a startled Jim in the forest; pitiful, wild-eyed

pages.text: Ben Gunn told me a secret. He whispered that he knew a great deal about the treasure on this island, more than the pirates guessed. If I and my friends would help him get safely home, he would be our friend and helper. I did not yet understand how important this lonely, half-mad man would turn out to be.

image.note: Ben Gunn speaking low and earnestly to Jim, gesturing towards the hills; a secret shared; the beginning of a bargain

pages.text: While I was away, my friends had found an old wooden fort, a stockade, on the island, and taken shelter inside it. I ran to join them there. The pirates soon attacked, swarming over the fence with cutlasses and pistols. It was a fierce and desperate fight, but we held the fort and drove them back, though not all of our brave men survived it.

image.note: A wooden log stockade defended by a few men; pirates storming the fence; a hard-fought battle, dramatic but not gory

pages.text: That night, I did another rash thing. I slipped away alone, found a small boat Ben Gunn had hidden, and rowed out to the Hispaniola in the dark to try to take back our ship. Aboard, I fought and outwitted a pirate who had been left to guard her, and, more by luck than skill, I ran the great ship aground in a quiet cove where the pirates could not reach her.

image.note: Jim alone at the wheel of the Hispaniola at night, steering the ship toward a moonlit cove; daring, tense

pages.text: When I crept back to the fort, I walked straight into the pirates, who had taken it while I was gone. They seized me. But Long John Silver, sensing that the tide was turning against him, cunningly chose to protect me, and used me to bargain for his own safety. Silver, I saw, served no one but himself, and would change sides whenever it suited him.

image.note: Jim held among rough pirates in the captured fort; Silver stepping between them, one arm out to shield the boy; scheming

pages.text: The pirates marched to the marked spot to dig up the gold, dragging me along. But when they tore open the ground, they found only an empty hole. The treasure was gone. The pirates howled with rage and turned on Silver, and in that dangerous moment, Doctor Livesey and his friends, with Ben Gunn, fell upon them from the trees and scattered them.

image.note: Pirates staring in fury into an empty pit; then men bursting from the trees to rout them; chaos, rescue

pages.text: For here was Ben Gunn's great secret. In his three lonely years on the island, he had found the treasure himself, dug it up, and carried it piece by piece to a cave of his own. The gold had been safe all along. The pirates had been digging for treasure that a marooned man had quietly moved years before they ever arrived.

image.note: A hidden cave heaped with gold coins and bars; Ben Gunn grinning proudly beside it; a wonderful surprise

pages.text: We carried the treasure down to the ship, load by heavy load. Long John Silver, still a prisoner, came with us, but on a night ashore he slipped away with a small bag of coins and was never seen again. I confess I was not entirely sorry. For all his wickedness, he had once been kind to me, and I did not like to think of him hanged.

image.note: The treasure being loaded onto the ship in sacks; Silver slipping off into darkness with a small bag; bittersweet

pages.text: We sailed home at last, our few brave survivors rich for life, and Ben Gunn given a share and his heart's wish, to see his home again. As for me, I had gold enough, but I had had adventure enough too. To this day, I never hear the sea break upon a shore without a shiver, and in my dreams a green parrot still cries, "Pieces of eight! Pieces of eight!"

image.note: Grown Jim at home years later, gazing out to sea, remembering; a faint parrot and island in his thoughts; wistful, closing
